Empirical Research Plan: “Are medium-sized Indian firms credit-constrained?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary design  : Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension, combined with an IV second stage to translate credit-supply shocks into real‐outcome effects.

Why DID?  
• The January-1998 rule change suddenly made firms with Plant & Machinery (P&M) investment between Rs 6.5 m and Rs 30 m eligible for subsidised “priority-sector” (PS) credit.  
• The January-2000 partial rollback removed eligibility for the Rs 10 m–Rs 30 m band.  
• Smaller firms (P&M ≤ 6.5 m) remained PS-eligible throughout and therefore provide a natural counterfactual.

Hence we observe the same firms before and after quasi-experimental shocks that alter only the bank’s willingness/price to lend, not the firm’s underlying demand for capital.  
The policy shocks were national, externally imposed, and the studied bank was right at the 40 % target, so the requirement was binding—perfect conditions for a supply-side experiment.

Two-stage extension  
Stage 1: DID estimates the causal effect of PS-eligibility on the amount/cost of working-capital credit (“first stage”).  
Stage 2: Use the exogenous portion of credit (predicted from stage 1) as an instrument (2SLS) for actual credit in profit or revenue regressions to obtain the marginal return to capital.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definitions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Running variable : Book value of P&M investment as of 1998 (measured in Rs million).

Discrete treatment variable  
   TREATi = 1 if 6.5 < P&M ≤ 30 in 1998  
      0 if P&M ≤ 6.5 (always PS-eligible “small” firms)

Event (timing) indicators  
Post98t = 1 for fiscal years 1998 and 1999 (full fiscal years after 1/98 change)  
Post00t = 1 for fiscal years 2000–2002 (after the 1/00 rollback)  

Main DID dummy  
   EligibleShockit = TREATi × Post98t  (1998–99 temporary eligibility)  

For the rollback we form  
   LostEligibilityit = TREATi × Post00t  (loss of eligibility from 2000 onward)

Control group : Firms with P&M ≤ 6.5 m—eligible both before and after, hence no change in supply conditions.

Note : In all regressions we include firm and year fixed effects so level differences in size or trend year effects are partialled out.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel pre-trends.  
 Absent the policy, medium (6.5–30) and small (≤ 6.5) firms would have followed similar trends in credit utilisation and real outcomes.  
 Plausibility: They operated in the same branches/regions; no earlier policy differentials. We will verify graphically and via placebo leads.

A2. No differential anticipation.  
 Firms did not adjust borrowing or investment in anticipation of the January-1998 rule (announced only weeks in advance) or the unexpected 2000 rollback. Large public-sector bank and sudden policy circulars make anticipation unlikely.

A3. Stable composition.  
 Sample membership is not systematically altered by the policy (e.g., attrition unrelated to treatment). Bank administrative panels suggest low exit and almost no deliberate closing of accounts.

A4. Exclusion in 2SLS.  
 PS-eligibility affects profits only through its impact on the supply/price of working-capital credit, not through other channels (e.g., direct tax breaks). The PS rules only affect banks’ lending quotas/prices.

A5. Stable Unit Treatment (no spillovers).  
 One firm’s change in eligibility does not materially affect another’s credit access because quotas are bank-wide and aggregate; the six‐region data dilute within-branch general‐equilibrium effects.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Differential demand shocks (e.g., sector-specific booms) coinciding with treatment.  
 Mitigation:  
 • Firm fixed effects and industry-year fixed effects.  
 • Pre-period placebo tests; test whether 1996→1997 differences already diverge.  
 • Event-study coefficients should be flat pre-1998.

Threat 2: Measurement error in P&M size category (1998 values might be manipulated).  
 Mitigation:  
 • Use the 1996–97 P&M book value (predates policy) when available.  
 • Drop firms with P&M very close (±0.5 m) to the 6.5 m threshold as robustness.  
 • Show balance tests on baseline covariates.

Threat 3: Sample attrition after 2000 (only 124 accounts in 2002).  
 Mitigation:  
 • Re-weight observations by inverse probability of staying in sample.  
 • Show results restricting to balanced panel 1996-2000 (pre-attrition window).  
 • Compare attrition rates across treatment/control.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The code uses `fixest` for high-dimensional FE and `ivreg` for 2SLS.

```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast feols and feols IV
library(modelsummary)

# 1. Data loading ----------------------------------------------------
dat <- fread("indian_firm_panel.csv")   # firm_id, year, pm_value, credit_limit, rate, sales, profit etc.

# 2. Variable construction ------------------------------------------
dat[, treat := as.integer(pm_value > 6.5 & pm_value <= 30)]      # medium firms
dat[, post98 := as.integer(year >= 1998 & year <= 1999)]
dat[, post00 := as.integer(year >= 2000)]
dat[, eligible_shock := treat * post98]
dat[, lost_elig    := treat * post00]

# Convenience log vars
dat[, l_credit := log(1 + credit_limit)]
dat[, l_sales  := log(1 + sales)]
dat[, l_profit := log(1 + profit)]

# 3. Main DID for credit supply -------------------------------------
did1 <- feols(l_credit ~ eligible_shock + treat + i(year) | firm_id + year, 
              data = dat, cluster = ~firm_id)
etable(did1, title = "Effect of PS eligibility on credit limit")

# Dynamic/event-study version
dat[, rel_year := year - 1998]  # relative to first shock
ev <- feols(l_credit ~ i(rel_year, treat, ref = -1) | firm_id + year,
            data = dat[year %between% c(1996,2002)], cluster = ~firm_id)

iplot(ev)   # pre-trend visual check

# 4. Two-Stage Least Squares (LATE of credit on profits) ------------
# First stage: l_credit on eligible_shock
# Second stage: l_profit on predicted l_credit
iv2 <- feols(l_profit ~ 1 | firm_id + year | l_credit ~ eligible_shock, 
             data = dat, cluster = ~firm_id)
etable(iv2, title = "IV estimate: marginal return to working capital")

# 5. Robustness: drop firms within 0.5m of size cut-off -------------
dat_rb <- dat[!(pm_value > 6 & pm_value < 7)]    # narrow band removed
did_rb <- feols(l_credit ~ eligible_shock | firm_id + year, 
                data = dat_rb, cluster = ~firm_id)
etable(list("Baseline"=did1, "No-close-to-cutoff"=did_rb))

# Save all tables
modelsummary::modelsummary(list(did1, iv2), output = "results.docx")
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Direction : Positive. Newly eligible medium firms should receive more working-capital credit at a slightly lower rate and, if previously constrained, convert this into higher sales and profits.

Magnitude : Prior studies (e.g., De Mel-McKenzie-Woodruff micro-SME) find real monthly returns to capital of 5 – 10 %. For somewhat larger manufacturing firms with working capital loans, I expect an annual ROI of 25 – 35 % (≈ 2 – 3 % per month) versus prevailing nominal loan rates of ~14 – 16 %. Hence the 2SLS coefficient of 0.25–0.35: a 1 % increase in working capital raises (log) annual profit by about 0.25–0.35 %.

Substitution : We anticipate about 50–60 % of extra credit substitutes for more expensive informal borrowing; the rest finances new production. This can be inferred from partial crowd-out of “other borrowing” accounts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Pre-treatment parallel trends visually & statistically verified ..... 0.8  
C2: No anticipation / timing exogeneity ................................ 1  
C3: No time-varying composition bias .................................... 0.7  
C4: No simultaneous confounding policies ................................ 0.8  
C5: Stable treatment, no interference (SUTVA) ........................... 0.9  

Average = 0.84 → Overall validity: Strong but still subject to the usual DID caveats.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
The outlined design exploits two sharp, externally imposed eligibility shocks, provides clear treatment and control groups, checks core assumptions, and supplies transparent code that can be expanded for robustness, heterogeneity, and welfare calculations.
